artiest/stanley-myers.text:
Stanley Myers was an English composer and conductor who wrote music for more than sixty films and television series. He was born in Birmingham in 1930 and studied at Oxford. In the early 1950s he worked as a songwriter and record producer, and in 1958 he first became involved in film music. In 1964 he wrote music for a Doctor Who serial, and he composed the theme for the BBC programme Question Time. He liked working with directors such as Nicolas Roeg, Jerzy Skolimowski and Volker Schlöndorff.

His best-known piece is Cavatina, a wistful guitar piece from 1970, written for the film The Walking Stick. The guitarist John Williams played it in the version that became the main theme of The Deer Hunter in 1978. For that piece Myers received an Ivor Novello Award. There is also a version with lyrics: Cleo Laine and Iris Williams sang it as He Was Beautiful. In 1966 he had the group Romeo Z record the title song for the film Kaleidoscope, and the Pink Floyd song Corporal Clegg from 1968 features brass players from his orchestra. He also composed for the horror films of Pete Walker.

In the 1980s he often worked with the director Stephen Frears. His music for Prick Up Your Ears won a prize at the Cannes Film Festival in 1987, and for The Witches he won another Ivor Novello Award in 1991. He was one of the first people to work with Hans Zimmer and introduced him to the trade. Myers died of cancer in London in 1993.
artiest/stanley-myers.listen: Listen to Cavatina in the version by John Williams. Notice the slow melody on the guitar and how the accompaniment stays simple, so that the piece sounds almost like a song.

artiest/stardust.text:
Stardust was a French house trio with a single song to their name: Music Sounds Better with You, released on 20 July 1998. The group consisted of Thomas Bangalter of Daft Punk, the DJ Alan Braxe and the singer Benjamin Diamond. Braxe and Diamond had met at boarding school and bonded there over music. Braxe gave Bangalter a demo of Vertigo, which Bangalter released in 1997 on his label Roulé. For a gig at the Rex Club in Paris, with Bangalter on keyboards and Diamond as singer, they still needed one more track. They wanted to write a song, not a pure club track.

They made the track in six days in Bangalter's home studio, Daft House, with a sampled guitar loop from Chaka Khan's Fate from 1981, a Rhodes piano, a Roland TR-909 and a bass from a Korg Trident. The lyrics, written by all three, are according to Diamond a mantra that anyone can understand. The record first appeared as a vinyl single for DJs. After being handed out at the Winter Music Conference in Miami, demand grew, and Virgin released it. It reached number two in the United Kingdom, number one in Greece and Spain, and the top of Billboard's dance chart. The video, directed by Michel Gondry, shows a boy building a model glider while the group performs on television wearing metal masks. More than two million copies were sold worldwide.

Stardust performed once more and then split up. Bangalter turned down an offer of three million dollars for an album. The track proves that repetition and simplicity can make a dance record shine: a gliding guitar figure, a warm bass line and a voice that returns like a mantra.
artiest/stardust.listen: Listen to Music Sounds Better with You and notice the guitar loop that keeps returning and the warm bass line underneath. Hear how little changes, and how the track nevertheless keeps gliding onwards.

artiest/stargate.text:
Stargate is a Norwegian production and songwriting duo consisting of Tor Erik Hermansen and Mikkel Storleer Eriksen, both born in 1972 and now based in Los Angeles. It began in 1996 in Trondheim as a trio, with Hallgeir Rustan as well. Hermansen was then working as a talent scout for Warner Music, Eriksen had a studio, and Rustan was a mechanical engineer. One of their first successes was the album Curious by the Norwegian R&B singer Noora Noor. For the British market they used the name Stargate.

Their first international success came with S Club 7 and the song S Club Party in 1999, followed by The Way to Your Love by Hear'Say in 2001. They also wrote and produced for Blue, Mis-Teeq and Atomic Kitten. Their method was to remix American hip hop and R&B and add layers of melody to it that suited European radio. When Hermansen and Eriksen decided to go to America, Rustan stayed in Norway. Their breakthrough in the United States came in 2006 with So Sick by Ne-Yo, which went to number one on the Billboard Hot 100.

After that they made a string of worldwide hits, including Irreplaceable by Beyoncé and Firework by Katy Perry. They worked a great deal with Rihanna, on songs such as Unfaithful, Don't Stop the Music, Rude Boy, Only Girl (In the World), What's My Name?, S&M and Diamonds. In 2013 they made Almost Home for Mariah Carey. The music is smooth, melodic pop with R&B rhythms, made for the radio. Stargate shows how much of the sound of pop in the 2000s and 2010s was created in the studios of producers.
artiest/stargate.listen: Listen to Irreplaceable by Beyoncé. Notice how simple the accompaniment is, with a gentle guitar and a steady rhythm, so that the vocals and the melody have all the space.

artiest/static-major.text:
Static Major, real name Stephen Ellis Garrett Jr., was an American producer, singer and songwriter from Louisville, Kentucky. He was born in 1974 and died in 2008, at the age of thirty-three. Earlier he performed under the name Static. In 1990 he founded the R&B trio Playa. That group belonged to Swing Mob, a musical collective from Virginia led by DeVanté Swing. Playa signed with Def Jam and attracted attention in 1998 with the single Cheers 2 U.

His greatest influence was as a writer. Together with Timbaland, also of Swing Mob, he wrote Pony by Ginuwine from 1996, and Are You That Somebody? by Aaliyah from 1998. After that he became Aaliyah's most important songwriter. He co-wrote Try Again from 2000, her only number 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, and almost all the songs on her third album Aaliyah from 2001. He also contributed to the debut album Make It Hot by Nicole Wray. Speaking about his inspiration, he said that he looked to the streets: if a song could not be played in the neighbourhood, it did not work for him.

In 2008 Lil Wayne's Lollipop was released, a song he co-wrote and on which he can be heard. It went to number one on the Billboard Hot 100. He died in February of that year as a result of a medical procedure, and the music video is dedicated to his memory. His voice returned later too, including on Aaliyah's Poison, in 2021, where he sings in the background.
artiest/static-major.listen: Listen to Lollipop by Lil Wayne. Notice the vocal part with a distorted voice in the background and how the low, slow beat carries the song.

artiest/stealers-wheel.text:
Stealers Wheel was a Scottish folk rock band from Paisley, formed in 1972 by two old school friends, Joe Egan and Gerry Rafferty. That same year the group signed to A&M Records. The first album Stealers Wheel came out in October 1972, produced by the American songwriters and producers Leiber and Stoller. It received good reviews and also sold well. Remarkably, Rafferty left the band just before its release, after which Luther Grosvenor replaced him on tour.

The most famous song is Stuck in the Middle with You. In 1973 it reached number six on the American Hot 100 and number eight in the United Kingdom. Rafferty was persuaded to return, but the other members left, and the band became a duo with changing backing musicians. The singles Everyone's Agreed That Everything Will Turn Out Fine and, in 1974, Star followed. The second album Ferguslie Park from 1973, named after a district of Paisley, was a commercial failure. The music is acoustic folk pop, with Beatles-like melodies and layered vocals, complemented by guitar, harmonica and piano.

Because of tensions between Egan and Rafferty and business problems, the band stopped in 1975, around the time of the third album Right or Wrong. The song Stuck in the Middle with You lived on when Quentin Tarantino used it in 1992 in his debut film Reservoir Dogs, in a notorious scene. Louise made a dance version of it in 2001. In 2008 the band briefly got together again, without Egan and Rafferty. Rafferty died in 2011 and Egan in 2024.
artiest/stealers-wheel.listen: Listen to Stuck in the Middle with You. Notice the half-sung, almost shaky vocals and how the rhythm keeps bouncing along, even in the quieter parts.

artiest/steel-pulse.text:
Steel Pulse is a British roots reggae band from Handsworth, a district of Birmingham. The group came together at Handsworth Wood Boys School and was formed in 1975 by, among others, the singer and guitarist David Hinds and the guitarist Basil Gabbidon, inspired by Catch a Fire by Bob Marley and the Wailers. The first single was Kibudu, Mansetta And Abuku, followed by Nyah Luv. Because the members were Rastafarians, they were at first unable to get gigs in Birmingham's Caribbean clubs. They therefore began playing at punk venues, such as the Hope and Anchor in London, and joined Rock Against Racism.

On Island Records came the single Ku Klux Klan, about racism, which in concert was accompanied by a parody of the sect. The debut album Handsworth Revolution came out in 1978 and was seen as a step in the development of roots reggae outside Jamaica. In 1982 the group founded its own label, Wise Man Doctrine, and released True Democracy. Earth Crisis followed in 1984, and then Babylon the Bandit, with which the band won a Grammy. Steel Pulse was the first non-Jamaican group to win the Grammy for best reggae album. Later came albums such as State of Emergency, Victims, Vex, Rage and Fury and Mass Manipulation.

The lyrics deal with racism, oppression and African heritage, in a warm reggae sound with keyboards, guitar and multi-part vocals. On 21 May 1981, the night of Bob Marley's funeral, the band played a concert in Washington that was broadcast worldwide. For reggae in Britain and in the United States, Steel Pulse was thus an important voice.
artiest/steel-pulse.listen: Listen to Ku Klux Klan. Notice how the calm reggae beat and the heavy bass contrast with the sharp lyrics about racism.

artiest/steely-dan.text:
Steely Dan is the duo of singer and keyboard player Donald Fagen and guitarist and bass player Walter Becker. They met in 1967 at Bard College in Annandale-on-Hudson, in New York State, and started the band in 1971. The name comes from the novel Naked Lunch by William S. Burroughs. Steely Dan showed how far you can take jazz harmony into a pop song without the song ceasing to be a pop song.

The debut Can't Buy a Thrill (1972) produced the hits Do It Again and Reelin' in the Years. After that the band increasingly became a studio project. After July 1974 Becker and Fagen no longer performed live. They recorded with constantly changing session musicians, with Gary Katz as producer. The high point of this way of working is Aja (1977). On the title track, nearly eight minutes long, the players include drummer Steve Gadd and saxophonist Wayne Shorter of Weather Report. The album reached number 3 on the American album chart and became the band's first platinum record. After Gaucho (1980), Becker and Fagen split up in 1981.

In 1993 they went on tour together again. The album Two Against Nature won the Grammy for Album of the Year in 2001, and in that same year Steely Dan was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Walter Becker died in 2017. The band's polished studio sound found its way into hip hop: De La Soul built Eye Know (1989) on a sample from Peg.
artiest/steely-dan.listen: Aja (1977): listen to the long middle section. First Wayne Shorter plays a saxophone solo, then comes the drum solo by Steve Gadd, the first drum solo on a Steely Dan song. The solo was edited together from two takes.

artiest/stefan-wolpe.text:
Stefan Wolpe was a German-born American composer. He was born in Berlin in 1902 to Jewish parents and studied with, among others, Franz Schreker and Ferruccio Busoni. Around 1923 he came into contact with the Bauhaus and with the Dadaists, and he set a poem by Kurt Schwitters to music. In 1928 his first opera, Zeus und Elida, premiered in Berlin. As a socialist he also wrote pieces for trade unions and communist theatre groups, in a more accessible style with influences from jazz and popular music.

After the Nazis seized power in 1933 he had to flee as a Jew and a communist. Via Vienna, where he took lessons from Anton Webern, he went to Palestine, where he wrote simple songs for kibbutzim and wanted to bring together Western, Eastern and Arabic music. In 1938 he settled in New York. From 1952 to 1956 he headed the music department of Black Mountain College, where Enactments for Three Pianos, among other works, came into being. His style remained eclectic: sometimes twelve-tone, sometimes diatonic, sometimes based on Arabic scales.

Wolpe was also an influential teacher. His students included Morton Feldman, David Tudor, Gil Evans and George Russell, so both avant-gardists and jazz musicians. He befriended Abstract Expressionist painters in New York. Elliott Carter said of his music that he does everything wrong and that it still turns out right. Wolpe developed Parkinson's disease in 1964 and died in 1972.
artiest/stefan-wolpe.listen: Listen to a short chamber piece by Wolpe, for example from Four Generations. Notice how sharply and unpredictably the notes alternate, and try to hear where jazzy rhythms crop up.

artiest/stella-chiweshe.text: Stella Chiweshe learned to play the mbira between 1966 and 1969 from her great-uncle, after other teachers had refused a woman. The mbira, a thumb piano with metal tines on a resonating box, belongs to the Shona ceremonies in which ancestors are invoked. In 1974 her single Kasahwa was released, and later she performed a great deal in Europe, especially in Germany. In this way she paved the way for female mbira players.
artiest/stella-chiweshe.listen: Listen to Kasahwa and hear how two hands play two interlocking patterns, with a softly rattling sound of shells or bottle caps.

artiest/stephane-grappelli.text: Stéphane Grappelli grew up in Paris and taught himself to play the violin. As a young musician he played in cinemas and dance orchestras. In 1934 he founded the Quintette du Hot Club de France with Django Reinhardt, in which his elegant, swinging violin counterbalanced Reinhardt's guitar. He was one of the first to make the violin sound like a fully fledged jazz instrument. When war broke out, he stayed in London, where he played with the young pianist George Shearing. After the war he occasionally played with Reinhardt again. In the 1970s he had a second career and made records with the classical violinist Yehudi Menuhin. He kept performing until shortly before his death in 1997.
artiest/stephane-grappelli.listen: Notice the violin dancing lightly and playfully above the rhythm guitars.

artiest/stephen-cleobury.text:
Sir Stephen Cleobury was an English organist and conductor. He was born in Bromley, Kent, in 1948, sang as a chorister at Worcester Cathedral and was an organ scholar at Cambridge. He then became sub-organist of Westminster Abbey and in 1979 the first Anglican director of music of the Catholic Westminster Cathedral. In 1982 he succeeded Philip Ledger as director of music of the Choir of King's College, Cambridge. He remained in that post until 2019. He died of cancer in November of that year.

The choir of King's College is world-famous for its Christmas music: since 1928 the BBC has broadcast the Festival of Nine Lessons and Carols live on Christmas Eve. Cleobury made the choir better known still through tours and recordings. His most important innovation was that from 1984 onwards he had a new carol written every year, by, among others, Thomas Adès, John Tavener and Mark-Anthony Turnage. The carol The Gleam by Harrison Birtwistle, in which the choristers have to stamp and shout, caused some controversy. He also broadened the repertoire with more Latin music and composers such as Kodály, Janáček and Arvo Pärt.

Besides King's, he conducted the Cambridge University Musical Society from 1983 to 2009 and the BBC Singers from 1995 to 2007. His albums include Miserere, Dixit Dominus, Requiems and Quattro pezzi sacri. From 1990 to 1992 he was president of the Royal College of Organists. His influence lies above all in the choral sound that many people associate with English Christmas music, and in the way he brought contemporary choral music to a large audience.
artiest/stephen-cleobury.listen: Listen to a recording of the choir of King's College under Cleobury, for example Spem in Alium by Thomas Tallis. Notice how the voices float in layers through the space of the chapel.

artiest/stephen-drury.text:
Stephen Drury is an American pianist, conductor and electronic musician. He was born in Spokane, Washington State, in 1955. His teachers included Margaret Ott, Patricia Zander and Claudio Arrau. In 1976 he graduated from Harvard, and then he studied for a year at the Juilliard School with William Masselos. Most of his career has been centred on Boston, where the Boston Globe called him the local authority on new music.

In the 1980s he was music director of the American Repertory Theater. He directs the contemporary music ensemble Callithumpian Consort, teaches at the New England Conservatory and since 2018 has been professor of piano for contemporary classical music at the Boston Conservatory at Berklee. He has played and recorded works by Stravinsky, Charles Ives, John Cage, Frederic Rzewski, Elliott Carter and John Zorn.

Most praised is his 1994 recording of The People United Will Never Be Defeated! by Rzewski, which critics regard as the definitive performance of that work. In 2008 he performed with Rzewski himself at Carnegie Hall. His recording of Carny by John Zorn is likewise considered definitive. For many listeners Drury is thus the pianist who makes the most difficult contemporary pieces accessible, including in his series of piano works by John Cage.
artiest/stephen-drury.listen: Listen to a section of The People United Will Never Be Defeated! in Drury's performance. Notice how a simple theme is varied again and again and how the pianist builds it up from soft to fierce.

artiest/stephen-foster.text:
Stephen Collins Foster was born in 1826 in Lawrenceville, Pennsylvania, and is sometimes called the father of American music. He wrote more than two hundred songs, mainly parlour music and folk music from the Romantic period. As a child he taught himself to play the clarinet, drum, flute, guitar and piano. At thirteen he took lessons from the German music dealer Henry Kleber in Pittsburgh, with whom he studied works by Mozart, Beethoven and Schubert.

After his marriage in 1850 he wrote most of his best-known songs: Camptown Races and Nelly Bly in 1850, Old Folks at Home, also known as Swanee River, in 1851, My Old Kentucky Home in 1853 and Jeanie with the Light Brown Hair in 1854. Oh! Susanna, Hard Times Come Again No More and Beautiful Dreamer are also his. Many of his songs were sung in the blackface minstrel shows that were popular in his day. Foster tried to make the lyrics more decent, but the genre was offensive to Black Americans even in his own time. After the early 1850s he wrote mainly parlour songs. Many songs have a Southern theme, but Foster never lived in the South and visited it only once.

He spent his last four years in New York. He fell ill, possibly fell in his hotel, and died in 1864, at the age of thirty-seven, in Bellevue Hospital. In his wallet was a note with the words Dear friends and gentle hearts. Many of his melodies remained popular, also in the twenty-first century, and form a foundation of the American song repertoire.
artiest/stephen-foster.listen: Listen to Beautiful Dreamer or Camptown Races. Notice the simple, singable melody that you can whistle along to after hearing it just once.

artiest/stephen-morris.text:
Stephen Morris was born in 1957 in Macclesfield, Cheshire. His father was a travelling salesman and organised dance evenings, and an uncle was a musician. He went to the same school as Ian Curtis, the future singer of Joy Division. After the band, still called Warsaw at the time, had already tried three other drummers, Morris answered an advertisement in a music shop and got the job.

Morris is known for his almost machine-like way of drumming. He attributes this to krautrock, and names Klaus Dinger of Neu! as an important example. He also admires Jaki Liebezeit of Can and Moe Tucker of The Velvet Underground, because they kept things simple. When recording Joy Division, producer Martin Hannett made him record every drum separately, so that Hannett had complete control over the sound. From early on he combined ordinary drumming with drum machines, a mixture that later returned in the music of New Order. Besides drums, he also plays keyboards and synthesizer.

After Curtis's death in 1980 Morris carried on in New Order, where together with Bernard Sumner he can be heard on every album. With his girlfriend and later wife Gillian Gilbert he made two albums as The Other Two. He also played with Bad Lieutenant and in 2010 made Swing. In the course he turns up in the story of the sleeve of Unknown Pleasures, the discovery of which some sources attribute to him. In 2026 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a member of Joy Division and New Order.
artiest/stephen-morris.listen: Listen to a Joy Division song and focus only on the drums. Notice how tight and regular the rhythm stays, almost like a machine.

artiest/stephen-sondheim.text:
Stephen Sondheim was an American composer and lyricist. He was born in New York in 1930, into a wealthy Jewish family, and died in 2021. As a teenager he became friends with James Hammerstein, the son of Oscar Hammerstein II. Hammerstein became a kind of foster father to him and awakened his love of musical theatre. Sondheim began as a lyricist for West Side Story in 1957 and Gypsy in 1959. After that he also wrote the music himself.

His best-known musicals are A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum, Company, Follies, A Little Night Music, Pacific Overtures, Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street, Merrily We Roll Along, Sunday in the Park with George, Into the Woods, Assassins and Passion. Company, A Little Night Music, Sweeney Todd and Passion won a Tony Award for best musical, and Sunday in the Park with George won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama. For the song Sooner or Later from Dick Tracy he received an Oscar. Much of his work was adapted for the screen, such as Sweeney Todd in 2007 and Into the Woods in 2014. He often worked with the director Harold Prince and later with James Lapine.

Sondheim's music and lyrics are complex, ambivalent and refined. His musicals deal with the darker sides of life, far beyond the usual subjects of the genre. For that reason he is seen as someone who reinvented the American musical. He received eight Tony Awards, eight Grammys, the Presidential Medal of Freedom and a Kennedy Center Honor. Theatres in New York and London bear his name.
artiest/stephen-sondheim.listen: Listen to a song from West Side Story, for which Sondheim wrote the lyrics. Notice how exactly the words fall into the rhythm of Bernstein's music and how the song tells a story.

artiest/steppenwolf.text:
Steppenwolf was an American rock band, formed in Los Angeles in 1967 by the singer and rhythm guitarist John Kay, the keyboard player Goldy McJohn and the drummer Jerry Edmonton, who had previously played in the Canadian group The Sparrows. The guitarist Michael Monarch and the bass player Rushton Moreve were found through advertisements in music shops. At the end of 1967 the producer Gabriel Mekler suggested renaming the group after the 1927 novel Steppenwolf by Hermann Hesse. The first singles were A Girl I Knew and Sookie Sookie.

The breakthrough came in 1968 with Born to Be Wild, and with their version of The Pusher by Hoyt Axton. Both songs are on the self-titled debut album and were heard prominently in the 1969 film Easy Rider. After that came Magic Carpet Ride from The Second, which reached number three on the Billboard Hot 100, and Rock Me from At Your Birthday Party, which reached number ten. The album Monster from 1969 was the group's most political record, criticising American policy in Vietnam. In 1971 For Ladies Only appeared. In 1972 the band gave a farewell concert in Los Angeles. In 1974 it returned with Slow Flux. Steppenwolf sold more than twenty-five million records and had thirteen singles on the Billboard Hot 100.

The sound consists of heavy, bluesy rock with Kay's raw voice, a sharp guitar and a driving organ part. The band is known as one of the early hard rock groups. In 2018 the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame chose Born to Be Wild as one of the first singles to be recognised.
artiest/steppenwolf.listen: Listen to Born to Be Wild and notice the heavy guitar riff and the driving rhythm that seems to imitate the engine. Can you hear how John Kay's voice sounds raw and defiant?

artiest/steve-coleman.text:
Steve Coleman is an American saxophonist, composer, bandleader and music theorist. He was born in 1956 and grew up on the South Side of Chicago. He began playing the alto saxophone at fourteen and later studied in Illinois and at Roosevelt University. In 1978 he moved to New York, where he played in the big bands of Thad Jones and Mel Lewis, Slide Hampton and Sam Rivers, and as a sideman with, among others, David Murray, Dave Holland, Michael Brecker and Abbey Lincoln.

In his first years in New York he played on the street and in small clubs with a group he put together with the trumpeter Graham Haynes. Out of that grew Steve Coleman and Five Elements, his most important ensemble. In it he developed improvisation within nested, repeating structures. Together with young Black musicians such as Cassandra Wilson and Greg Osby he founded the M-Base movement. Albums from that period include Back to the Beautiful, Phase Space, Rhythm in Mind and Flashback on M-Base.

Coleman sees his music as part of the African diaspora and searched for those roots. In 1993 he travelled to Ghana and became interested in the polyrhythms of the Dagomba. In 1996 he worked for twelve days with the Cuban group Afrocuba de Matanzas and recorded The Sign and the Seal. In 1997 he travelled to Senegal and in 1998 to southern India. In 2014 he received a MacArthur Fellowship. His influence on jazz can be heard above all in the way young musicians approach rhythm and structure.
artiest/steve-coleman.listen: Listen to a track from Rhythm in Mind or Phase Space. Notice how the rhythm keeps shifting and how the melodies pass through the band in short, repeated figures.

artiest/steve-cropper.text:
Steve Cropper was an American guitarist, songwriter and producer. He was born in Dora, Missouri, in 1941, and moved as a child to Memphis, where he got to know Black gospel music. He got his first guitar at fourteen. He admired, among others, Chuck Berry, Jimmy Reed and Chet Atkins. With the guitarist Charlie Freeman he started the Mar-Keys, who were named after the sign above the Stax Records studio and had a hit in 1961 with Last Night.

At Stax, Cropper became one of the founders of the house band Booker T. & the M.G.'s, with Booker T. Jones on Hammond organ, drummer Al Jackson Jr. and later bass player Donald Duck Dunn. In 1962 they had a hit of their own with Green Onions. The band also played on records by Otis Redding, Wilson Pickett, Sam & Dave and Carla Thomas. Cropper played a Fender Esquire and later a Telecaster. He was known for short, dry chords and sparse licks: he never played a note too many. He co-wrote In the Midnight Hour with Wilson Pickett, Knock on Wood with Eddie Floyd and (Sittin' On) the Dock of the Bay with Otis Redding. In Sam & Dave's Soul Man he is even mentioned by name.

After leaving Stax in 1970 he worked with, among others, Rod Stewart, Ringo Starr and Jeff Beck. Later he played in the Blues Brothers Band, including in the films. In 1992 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with the M.G.'s. He died in 2025.
artiest/steve-cropper.listen: Listen to Green Onions by Booker T. & the M.G.'s from 1962. Notice how the organ plays the blues riff, while Cropper's guitar adds short stabs and plays a sharp solo halfway through.

artiest/steve-gadd.text:
Steve Gadd, in full Stephen Kendall Gadd, is an American drummer and session musician, born in 1945 and raised in Irondequoit in New York State. He began drumming as a boy. At eleven he won a talent contest and played on The Mickey Mouse Club. He studied at the Eastman School of Music and then spent three years in the Army Field Band. He made his first studio recording in 1968.

In 1973 he briefly formed the jazz fusion group L'Image and played on many records on the jazz label CTI, including for Milt Jackson, Chet Baker and Jim Hall. Later in the 1970s he started the group Stuff. Well-known recordings include Paul Simon's 50 Ways to Leave Your Lover, Herbie Mann's Hi-jack and above all the title track Aja by Steely Dan from 1977, on which his drum solo at the end has become legendary. He also worked with Chick Corea, Eric Clapton, James Taylor, Paul McCartney and David Gilmour. In 1984 he was inducted into the Modern Drummer Hall of Fame.

Gadd is regarded as one of the most highly valued session drummers, because he knew how to find exactly the right groove for a song, in widely differing styles. In the course he appears in the chapter on the jazz festival: while Wayne Shorter plays a saxophone solo, Gadd plays a solo while the band carries on around him.
artiest/steve-gadd.listen: Listen to Aja by Steely Dan and notice the drum solo at the end, with the fast tom runs and the clear cymbals. How does the groove stay upright while the rest of the band carries on playing?

artiest/steve-harris.text:
Steve Harris is an English bass player and songwriter, best known as the founder of the heavy metal band Iron Maiden. He was born in Leytonstone, then still part of Essex, in 1956. As a boy he wanted to become a professional footballer and even trained at West Ham United. Then he discovered rock music, above all through The Beatles. He wanted to play drums, but had no room at home for a drum kit and therefore chose the bass guitar, which he taught himself to play. His first bass was a copy of a 1971 Fender Precision. He played in small bands, including Smiler, where his songs were found too complicated.

In 1975 he founded Iron Maiden. The name comes from the film The Man in the Iron Mask. Until the contract with EMI in 1979 he worked as an architectural draughtsman and later as a street sweeper. He is the only one who has been in the band the whole time, and together with the guitarist Dave Murray he played on all the studio albums. In the early days he wrote almost all the music and lyrics. His lyrics often deal with mythology and history, and with books and films. Later came keyboards, backing vocals, co-production and the direction of live videos. With British Lion he made a hard rock side project, with the album British Lion from 2012.

For the history of pop his bass playing is the most important thing. He developed an influential style, the gallop, a fast, rolling bass pattern that can be heard on Run to the Hills and The Trooper. He also brought progressive changes of time signature and tempo into heavy metal. He is regarded as one of the best metal bass players ever.
artiest/steve-harris.listen: Listen to The Trooper by Iron Maiden. Notice the bass that races through the song like a galloping horse, with short, fast notes beneath the guitars.

artiest/steve-jones.text:
Steve Jones, in full Stephen Philip Jones, is an English guitarist, born in 1955 in Shepherd's Bush in London. He grew up with his young mother, who was a hairdresser, and his grandparents. As a child he became friends with Paul Cook. He rarely went to school and often got into trouble with the police. Later he said that the Sex Pistols saved him from a life of crime.

Jones is best known as the guitarist of the punk band Sex Pistols, with whom he released Anarchy in the UK in 1976. After the group broke up he started the group The Professionals with former bandmate Paul Cook. He released two solo albums, Mercy in 1987 and Fire and Gasoline in 1989, and worked with, among others, Johnny Thunders, Iggy Pop, Cheap Trick, Bob Dylan and Thin Lizzy. In 1995 he briefly formed the supergroup Neurotic Outsiders, with members of Guns N' Roses and Duran Duran. In 2015 Rolling Stone placed him at number 97 on its list of the hundred best guitarists.

His guitar sound is thick and full. What seems simple at first hearing is not: he double-tracked the guitar parts, so that a wall of sound results. In the course this appears as a listening tip for Anarchy in the UK, the song that shows how raw and yet carefully made punk could be.
artiest/steve-jones.listen: Listen to Anarchy in the UK and notice the guitars, which together form a dense wall of sound. Can you hear that it is two identical parts, layered on top of each other?

artiest/steve-lacy.text:
Steve Lacy, born Steven Norman Lackritz, was an American jazz saxophonist and composer, one of the most important players of the soprano saxophone. He was born in 1934 and died in 2004. At sixteen he was already playing Dixieland with older musicians such as Red Allen and Pee Wee Russell. He then moved into the avant-garde: he played on Jazz Advance from 1956, Cecil Taylor's debut album, and in 1957 performed with Taylor's quartet at the Newport Jazz Festival.

His longest bond was with the music of Thelonious Monk. In 1958 he recorded Reflections, the first album consisting solely of Monk's compositions, and in 1960 he played briefly in Monk's band. Monk is on almost every Lacy album and concert programme, often together with the trombonist Roswell Rudd. He also played works by Mingus, Ellington and Herbie Nichols, and rarely ordinary pop songs. In 1965 he came to Europe, and in 1970 he moved to Paris, where he lived until the last two years of his life.

From the 1970s to the 1990s his work centred on his sextet, with his wife, the singer and violinist Irene Aebi. He also became a specialist in solo saxophone. His music is melodic and tightly constructed, often built from little more than a single questioning phrase that repeats. He made music for poems by Robert Creeley, Samuel Beckett and haiku, and worked with painters and dancers. In 1992 he received a MacArthur Fellowship. In the United States he remained less well known than in Europe.
artiest/steve-lacy.listen: Listen to a Monk composition on Reflections: Steve Lacy Plays Thelonious Monk. Notice the clear, thin sound of the soprano sax and how the angular melody is repeated like a question.

artiest/steve-lillywhite.text:
Steve Lillywhite is an English record producer, born in Surrey in 1955. He began in 1972 as a tape operator at Phonogram Studios in London. A demo he made for Ultravox earned that band a contract with Island Records, and Lillywhite became its regular producer. His first success came in 1978 with Hong Kong Garden, the debut single by Siouxsie and the Banshees, followed by their album The Scream. In that year he also produced Ku Klux Klan, Steel Pulse's first single on Island. In 1979 he made the album Drums and Wires with XTC, with the single Making Plans for Nigel.

In 1980 he produced Peter Gabriel's third solo album. Together with Gabriel and the sound engineer Hugh Padgham he came up with the gated reverb drum sound there, which later became a hallmark of Phil Collins's solo records. That same year Boy, U2's debut album, came out. With U2 he went on to make October, War and The Joshua Tree. In 1987 he produced Fairytale of New York by The Pogues, with his wife Kirsty MacColl as the female vocalist. The song just missed the top spot on the British Christmas chart and returns every year over the holidays.

In the 1990s he worked with the Dave Matthews Band, including the album Under the Table and Dreaming, and later with, among others, Counting Crows, Phish, Morrissey and The Killers. He is credited on more than five hundred records, won six Grammys and was made a CBE in 2012. His work shows how much of the sound of new wave and the big rock bands around 1980 was created in the studio.
artiest/steve-lillywhite.listen: Listen to Fairytale of New York by The Pogues. Notice how the song grows from quiet piano and vocals into a full, loud chorus, and how the two voices give each other room.

artiest/steve-mccall.text:
Steve McCall was an American jazz drummer. He was born in Chicago in 1933 and as a child had the chance to drum along in the annual Bud Billiken Parade. As a teenager he studied music theory and Latin American and classical percussion. After his time in the air force he returned to Chicago in 1954, bought his first drum kit and took lessons with Charles Specs Wright in Philadelphia. In 1961 he became friends with the pianist Muhal Richard Abrams and played in his Experimental Band. In 1965 he was one of the founders of the AACM, the Chicago organisation for innovative jazz, where he was at first treasurer.

In 1967 he moved to Amsterdam, as the first AACM member in Europe, and played with Don Byas and Dexter Gordon. In Paris he worked with Anthony Braxton, Leo Smith and Leroy Jenkins, and he was a link between the first European free jazz musicians and the AACM, including Willem Breuker, the Instant Composers Pool and John Surman. In 1970 he formed the Creative Construction Company with Braxton, Smith, Jenkins, Abrams and Richard Davis.

In 1975 he formed the trio Air in New York with Henry Threadgill and Fred Hopkins, which recorded eleven albums. He also played with Cecil Taylor, David Murray and Roscoe Mitchell. McCall never recorded a session of his own as leader. On Vintage Duets, recorded in 1980 and released in 1994, he shares top billing with the saxophonist Fred Anderson. He died in 1989. According to The Penguin Guide to Jazz he combined forward drive with outbursts of complete rhythmic anarchy, and Threadgill said that his treatment of space gave him freedom.
artiest/steve-mccall.listen: Listen to a recording by Air, the trio of Threadgill, Hopkins and McCall. Notice how McCall's drums do not keep a fixed metre, but use silence and unexpected accents.

artiest/steve-reich.text:
Steve Reich is an American composer who helped shape minimal music in the second half of the 1960s. He was born in New York in 1936, studied philosophy at Cornell University and then composition at Juilliard and Mills College, where Luciano Berio and Darius Milhaud were his teachers. His first breakthrough came with tape works. In It's Gonna Rain and Come Out he had two identical recordings of a spoken sentence slowly drift out of sync, so that a single sentence turned into a web of rhythms. This technique is called phase shifting.

In 1970 Reich travelled to Ghana to study the polyrhythmic music of the Ewe for five weeks. Drumming, a large work for percussion, voices and flutes, grew out of that. Later he studied Balinese gamelan. Both experiences resonate in Music for 18 Musicians, which he began in 1974 and which is based on a cycle of eleven chords. The piece is written for a larger ensemble with marimbas, xylophones, pianos, strings, clarinets and voices. It breathes, pulses and changes so gradually that the listener only notices the shifts afterwards.

In the 1980s his work took on a darker tone, with Jewish themes in Tehillim and historical themes in Different Trains. Reich's repeating patterns have had an effect on experimental music, rock and contemporary electronic music. That explains why the course mentions him on the road to minimalist thinking in pop music.
artiest/steve-reich.listen: Listen to the beginning of Music for 18 Musicians and notice the pulsing chords of the marimbas and pianos. Try to hear how each new chord change slowly announces itself, while the basis of the rhythm carries on.

artiest/steve-silk-hurley.text:
Steve Silk Hurley is an American club DJ, house producer and songwriter from Chicago, born in 1962. He studied engineering, but dropped out in 1981 to devote himself entirely to music. In the mid-1980s he became known as a DJ on the Chicago radio station WBMX, on the programme Saturday Night Live Ain't No Jive Dance Party. His mixing style went beyond beatmatching: he also used scratching, beat juggling and backspinning the record, techniques from hip hop.

With the singer Keith Nunnally he made a string of dance club hits as J. M. Silk, of which I Can't Turn Around reached the top of the American dance chart in 1986. That song was a cover of Isaac Hayes, and Hurley's housemate Farley Keith released a version of his own, over which they fell out. In January 1987 Jack Your Body spent two weeks at the top of the British singles chart, the first house hit to reach number 1 there, without having been played on BBC Radio 1 outside the chart programmes. After that he never had another hit under his own name. In 1988 the album Work It Out Compilation was released on Atlantic, and in 1997 he had one more British hit with The Word Is Love by The Voices of Life.

He is also an important remixer, including for Madonna, Michael Jackson, CeCe Peniston, New Order, Janet Jackson and Inner City, and has been nominated for a Grammy four times. For the history of pop he is above all the man who brought Chicago house to the general public.
artiest/steve-silk-hurley.listen: Listen to Jack Your Body. Notice how bare the track is: a tight drum machine, a low bass line and hardly any lyrics, and yet it keeps you dancing.

artiest/steve-stevens.text:
Steve Stevens, born Steven Bruce Schneider, is an American guitarist from New York. He was born in 1959 and grew up in Queens. He began playing guitar at seven, inspired by the folk singer Phil Ochs, got his first serious guitar with nylon strings at eight and an electric one only at thirteen. At the high school for music and the performing arts he became interested in classical guitar, with Steve Howe and Robert Fripp as examples. Flamenco also attracted him early on.

He is best known as the guitarist and writing partner of Billy Idol. When Idol came to New York after Generation X in 1981, his manager brought them together. With the producer Keith Forsey they formed the trio that defined Billy Idol in the 1980s. Together they made Billy Idol in 1982, Rebel Yell in 1983 and Whiplash Smile in 1986, all three multi-platinum. In 1988 they split up, and in 2001 they got back together. Devil's Playground in 2005 and Dream Into It in 2025 were among those that followed. In 2026 they were inducted together into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

With Harold Faltermeyer, Stevens made the Top Gun Anthem for the film Top Gun, for which he received a Grammy in 1987 for best pop instrumental performance. He also played for Michael Jackson, Ric Ocasek and Vince Neil, was a co-founder of Bozzio Levin Stevens and played flamenco guitar on Pistolero by Juno Reactor. His own albums include Atomic Playboys, Flamenco A Go-Go and Memory Crash.
artiest/steve-stevens.listen: Listen to Top Gun Anthem. Notice how the electric guitar carries the melody like a shining solo voice, above synthesizers and drums.

artiest/steve-strange.text:
Steve Strange, born Stephen John Harrington in 1959, was a Welsh singer and club host. He grew up in Wales and was gripped by punk in 1976 after seeing a Sex Pistols concert. In London he worked for Malcolm McLaren and sang in a few short-lived bands, but he soon grew tired of the punk scene.

His real influence lay elsewhere. Together with the DJ Rusty Egan he organised Bowie nights at Billy's in Soho in 1978. In 1979 they took over the Tuesday night at the Blitz, a wine bar in Covent Garden. Strange stood at the door himself and let in only people who looked remarkable: the individualistic, the eccentric, the beautifully dressed. In this way the Blitz grew into the cradle of the New Romantics, and its visitors were nicknamed the Blitz Kids. After the Blitz came Club for Heroes and, from 1982, the Camden Palace.

Alongside this, Strange was the singer of Visage, a group built around Rusty Egan, Midge Ure of Rich Kids, Billy Currie of Ultravox and a few members of Magazine. It began as a studio project, with the single Tar in 1979. In 1980 Strange appeared in the video for Ashes to Ashes by David Bowie. That same year Visage released Fade to Grey, a synthesizer record that reached number one in Germany and Switzerland. In 1985 the group broke up. Strange died in 2015. He remains the face of a scene in which clothing, club culture and synth-pop formed a single whole.
artiest/steve-strange.listen: Listen to Fade to Grey by Visage. Notice how the synthesizers carry the rhythm and the atmosphere, and how cool and distant the voice sounds.

artiest/steven-severin.text:
Steven Severin, born Steven John Bailey, is an English songwriter, composer, multi-instrumentalist and producer. He was born in 1955, grew up in Archway and moved to Bromley at the age of eleven. In 1971 he discovered the German band Can, and at fifteen he saw Captain Beefheart in London, which affected him deeply. His favourite writers were William Burroughs and Jean Genet. His name comes from a character of Sacher-Masoch's who is mentioned in Venus in Furs by The Velvet Underground.

In 1976 he founded Siouxsie and the Banshees with Siouxsie Sioux, as bass player. He co-wrote the music and supplied many lyrics, beginning with Voices, the B-side of Hong Kong Garden. With the group he recorded eleven studio albums. In 1983 he made the side project The Glove with Robert Smith of The Cure, with the album Blue Sunshine, an experimental whole with psychedelic and pop-art references, on which Jeanette Landray sings. The album reached number thirty-five on the British chart in 1983.

After the end of the Banshees in 1996 he founded his own label RE: and released instrumental albums through his website. He made music for silent films, such as The Woman in the Dunes, Vampyr and Blood Of A Poet, and in the late 2000s and early 2010s performed live solo to film footage. He continued to release albums later too, such as The Bedlam Variations in 2024. His work runs from post-punk to film music.
artiest/steven-severin.listen: Listen to Hong Kong Garden by Siouxsie and the Banshees. Notice the striking, tight bass line and the bright guitar fragments that together define the post-punk sound.

artiest/steven-tyler.text:
Steven Tyler, born Steven Tallarico, is the singer of the American rock band Aerosmith. He was born in New York in 1948 and grew up in the Bronx and Yonkers. His father was a classical pianist and music teacher. At seventeen he saw the Rolling Stones, and everyone said that with his big lips he looked like Mick Jagger. In 1964 he started his first band. In 1969 in New Hampshire he saw the guitarist Joe Perry and the bass player Tom Hamilton play. Around 1970 they started a band together, with Tyler as singer. With the drummer Joey Kramer and later the guitarist Brad Whitford they moved to Boston and it became Aerosmith.

In the 1970s Aerosmith became big with hard rock on albums such as Toys in the Attic and Rocks, and with singles such as Dream On, Sweet Emotion and Walk This Way. Tyler had written Dream On before the band even existed. He has a large vocal range and is known for his high, piercing screams. On stage he is an acrobat in colourful clothes, with scarves tied to his microphone stand. He also plays harmonica and keyboards.

At the end of the 1970s Tyler became addicted and the band declined. After rehab in 1986, he and Perry joined in on Run-DMC's new version of Walk This Way. That record brought rock and hip hop together and put Aerosmith back on the map. Successful albums such as Permanent Vacation, Pump and Get a Grip followed. In 2001 Tyler was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with Aerosmith.
artiest/steven-tyler.listen: Listen to Walk This Way by Run-DMC and Aerosmith from 1986. Notice the moment when Steven Tyler's piercing voice launches the chorus after the raps of Run and DMC.

artiest/steven-van-zandt.text:
Steven Van Zandt, born Steven Lento in 1950, grew up in New Jersey and hung around the club scene of the Jersey Shore from an early age. Around 1970 he became a friend of Bruce Springsteen and played with him in bands such as Steel Mill. Because of his Hawaiian shirts he got the nickname Miami Steve. He co-founded Southside Johnny and the Asbury Jukes, wrote many of their songs and produced their first records, including Hearts of Stone.

In 1975 he arranged the horns for Tenth Avenue Freeze-Out and contributed to the guitar line of Born to Run. On 20 July 1975 he officially became a member of the E Street Band, in which he played guitar and mandolin. In 1984 he left to go solo with Little Steven and the Disciples of Soul. On the album Voice of America his music became emphatically political. Since 1999 he has played with the E Street Band again. He also became known as an actor, including as Silvio Dante in The Sopranos.

For the course, his activism is what matters most. In 1985 he founded Artists United Against Apartheid, in response to the Sun City resort in South Africa. Forty-nine artists, including Springsteen, Bono, Bob Dylan, Peter Gabriel, Ringo Starr, Joey Ramone and Run DMC, recorded the song Sun City and declared in it that they would never perform there. In this way Van Zandt showed that a pop record can also be a political statement.
artiest/steven-van-zandt.listen: Listen to Sun City by Artists United Against Apartheid. Notice how many different voices and styles pass by, from rock to hip hop, and how the lyrics name the message again and again.

artiest/stevie-nicks.text:
Stevie Nicks, born in 1948 in Phoenix, Arizona, is a singer and songwriter. In California she met Lindsey Buckingham and sang with him in the psychedelic band Fritz. They then carried on as a duo. Their 1973 album Buckingham Nicks did not catch on, and Polydor dropped them. Nicks then worked as a waitress and cleaner, and in the meantime wrote the first versions of Rhiannon and Landslide.

In 1975 the drummer Mick Fleetwood asked Buckingham to join Fleetwood Mac. Buckingham made it a condition that Nicks could come too. The duo's harmonies gave the blues rock group an accessible pop sound. The album Fleetwood Mac from 1975 became a worldwide success, and Rumours followed as one of the best-selling albums of all time. It won a Grammy for Album of the Year in 1978. In 1981 Nicks began a solo career alongside the band with Bella Donna, which reached the top of the Billboard 200. It also included Edge of Seventeen. In 1998 she was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with Fleetwood Mac, and in 2019 as a solo artist.

Nicks is characterised by a husky, lived-in voice and lyrics with a mystical, almost fairy-tale tone. On stage she stood out with fluttering scarves and platform boots. For the course she is also the other face of a famous break-up: Buckingham wrote Go Your Own Way about their relationship, while she processed the same pain in her own songs.
artiest/stevie-nicks.listen: Listen to Go Your Own Way by Fleetwood Mac. Notice the voice of Lindsey Buckingham in the verses and the backing vocals of Nicks, who join him in the chorus.

artiest/stevie-wishart.text:
Stevie Wishart is a composer, improviser and performer on the hurdy-gurdy and the violin. She works mainly in contemporary music, but also has a career in early music. She edited and recorded the complete works of Hildegard of Bingen, and with her ensemble Sinfonye she plays music by medieval troubadours and trouvères and from the Cantigas de Santa Maria. She studied at Cambridge, Oxford and the Guildhall School of Music, and then composition and electronic music at the University of York. With John Cage and David Tudor she studied improvised and aleatoric music.

Wishart's work explores how music can express ideas that other forms of communication cannot reach. She made music for productions by Michèle Noiret and Wayne McGregor, for the designer Philippe Starck and for the BBC Proms, where the BBC Singers and Sinfonye performed her choral work Out of this World in 2011. She also wrote Rough with the Smooth, a concerto for double bass, in 2015, and the cantata The Seasons in 2014. She has performed at the Queen Elizabeth Hall and the Royal Festival Hall in London, the Sydney Opera House and St Peter's Basilica, and has recorded for Decca, Hyperion and Glossa.

Concern for the environment runs like a thread through her work. She is a member of the art-science network Fo.am and co-founder of the Ecotones Network. In her recent orchestral, chamber and vocal works she often uses the sounds of endangered species as a theme. In this way she connects an old instrument such as the hurdy-gurdy with the newest music and with the nature of today.
artiest/stevie-wishart.listen: Listen to a recording of Wishart on hurdy-gurdy, for example from Hildegard. Notice the buzzing, continuous drone beneath the melody, which gives a medieval atmosphere.

artiest/stevie-wishart-en-sinfonye.text:
Stevie Wishart is a composer, improviser and performer on the hurdy-gurdy and the violin. She studied at Cambridge, Oxford and the Guildhall School of Music and took lessons in composition and electronic music at York. Later she studied improvisation and aleatoric music with John Cage and David Tudor. She works mainly in contemporary music, but also built a career in early music.

With her ensemble Sinfonye she plays repertoire of the medieval troubadours and trouvères and from the Cantigas de Santa Maria. She also edited and recorded the complete works of Hildegard von Bingen. Her recordings have appeared on Decca Records, Hyperion and Glossa, among others. In this way she belongs to the musicians who bring medieval songs back to life with a sound of their own and plenty of imagination, rather than performing them as museum pieces.

In her own compositions Wishart searches for what music can express that other forms of communication cannot reach. She wrote for dance, theatre and choirs, and her work has been performed at, among other places, the Queen Elizabeth Hall in London and at the BBC Proms. Nature and the environment play a large role: in recent works she regularly uses the sounds of endangered species as a theme. In the course she appears as the performer of a song by Bernart de Ventadorn, a twelfth-century troubadour.
artiest/stevie-wishart-en-sinfonye.listen: Listen to Can vei la lauzeta mover and notice the hurdy-gurdy. Can you hear a sound that keeps droning beneath the singing, and how does it relate to the melody of the voice?

artiest/stevie-wonder.text:
Stevie Wonder was born Stevland Hardaway Judkins in 1950 in Saginaw, Michigan. He was born prematurely and was blinded by too much oxygen in the incubator. His mother moved with the children to Detroit, where he sang in a church choir and learned to play piano, harmonica and drums. Ronnie White of The Miracles heard him sing and arranged an audition at Motown. In 1961, at eleven, he signed to Tamla as Little Stevie Wonder.

In 1963 Fingertips, recorded live in Chicago, became a number 1 in America: he was thirteen. Hits followed such as Uptight (Everything's Alright), I Was Made to Love Her, For Once in My Life and Signed, Sealed, Delivered I'm Yours, the first song he produced himself. At twenty-one he let his contract with Motown run out. He forced through a new contract with far more artistic freedom. Together with Robert Margouleff and Malcolm Cecil and their enormous home-built synthesizer he made Music of My Mind and Talking Book (1972), with Superstition and You Are the Sunshine of My Life. Innervisions (1973), Fulfillingness' First Finale (1974) and Songs in the Key of Life (1976) followed.

On his records Wonder often played nearly all the instruments himself. With synthesizers and electronic keyboards he changed the sound of rhythm and blues in the 1970s, and he made albums that work as a whole, with lyrics about social issues. Like Marvin Gaye, he showed that a Motown artist could decide for himself what to record.
artiest/stevie-wonder.listen: Listen to Superstition and notice the clavinet, the electric keyboard instrument that plays the funky main motif. Hear how the drums start alone and how the horns later reinforce the motif.
